title: Wet but thirsty: how a root drinks, and why salty soil dries a plant

summary.text: A seedling standing in a flooded field can droop like a plant in the desert. Water is all around her roots, and she still cannot drink it. Water moves toward the place where it is held more tightly, and salt holds water tightly. Your child sprouts moong seeds in water with different amounts of salt, and finds where the sprouting stops. They then follow water along its whole path, from soil to root to leaf to air, and see that dry air does most of the pulling. They also meet the mangroves of the Sundarbans, which live in sea water.
summary.art: A split picture of a rice seedling in a wet field: on the left the seedling stands green in fresh water, on the right the same seedling droops in muddy salty water, with tiny arrows showing water leaving the root hairs.

intro.hook: Pour a glass of sea water on a potted plant. Within two days she droops, though her soil is soaking wet. How can a plant die of thirst while she stands in water?
intro.text: Try this at the table. Cut a cucumber into slices as thin as a coin. Lay ten slices on a plate and sprinkle a good pinch of salt over them. Come back in 20 minutes. There is a puddle on the plate, and the slices have gone floppy. The salt did not make that water. It came out of the cucumber. Whatever the salt does to a cucumber slice, it can also do to the roots of a plant.
intro.art: A white plate with ten cucumber slices dusted with salt, a small puddle around them, and one slice drooping over the edge of a spoon.

outcomes: I can explain that water moves toward the place where it is held more tightly, and that salt and thin films of water hold it tightly.
I can explain why a plant can wilt in soil that is wet with salty water.
I can describe how a root takes water in through root hairs, and why the root's cells must hold water tighter than the soil does.
I can describe the path of water through a plant as a slope from soil to leaf to dry air, and say where most of the drop happens.
I can explain how the holes in a leaf open and shut by the same movement of water.
I can plan a fair test with one change, and use the results to say how salty is too salty for a sprout.
I can tell the journey of water in the xylem apart from the journey of sugar in the phloem.
I can give two ways that plants such as mangroves live in salty or dry places.

terms.meaning: A number for how tightly water is held. A bigger pull number means a tighter hold. Scientists call the real thing water potential and write it with a minus sign.
terms.example: Water in a glass has a pull number of 0. Sea water is about 2.5.
terms.art: A glass of plain water labelled 0 next to a glass of sea water labelled 2.5, with a tiny hand gripping the water in the second glass.

terms.meaning: The movement of water through a thin skin toward the side where water is held more tightly.
terms.example: Salt on a cucumber slice pulls water out of the slice by osmosis.
terms.art: A cucumber slice with salt grains on top and small blue drops moving up out of the slice toward the salt.

terms.meaning: A very thin skin around every cell. It lets water through easily and holds back many dissolved things.
terms.example: The membrane around a root cell lets water in but keeps the sugars inside.
terms.art: A cut-away of a cell with a thin glowing skin, small water drops passing through and larger dots stopped outside.

terms.meaning: Mixed into water so well that you cannot see it any more, like salt in a glass of water.
terms.example: The salt in sea water is dissolved. You taste it but you cannot see it.
terms.art: A spoon of salt stirred into a glass of clear water, with the grains fading into nothing.

terms.meaning: A very thin tube that grows out of one cell on the outside of a young root. It takes in water.
terms.example: A moong sprout's root has a fuzz of white root hairs.
terms.art: A magnified young root covered in fine white hairs, pushing between brown soil grains.

terms.meaning: The firm push of a cell full of water against its own wall, like air pushing inside a tyre.
terms.example: Turgor keeps a fresh palak leaf stiff.
terms.art: Two cells side by side: a plump full cell pressing out on its wall, and a shrunken floppy cell pulling away from its wall.

terms.meaning: Drooping, because the plant's cells have lost water and lost their firm push.
terms.example: Coriander left on a counter wilts in an hour or two.
terms.art: A bunch of coriander drooping over the edge of a steel plate.

terms.meaning: The loss of water as vapour from a plant, mostly through tiny holes in the leaves.
terms.example: A bag tied over a leaf fills with tiny drops of transpired water.
terms.art: A clear bag tied over a leafy twig with fine droplets running down the inside.

terms.meaning: A tiny hole in a leaf, shaped like a mouth, that lets air in and water vapour out. The plural is stomata.
terms.example: A tulsi leaf has thousands of stomata on its underside.
terms.art: A magnified leaf surface with a mouth-shaped hole between two bean-shaped cells.

terms.meaning: One of the two bean-shaped cells around a stoma. They swell to open it and shrink to close it.
terms.example: In bright morning light, the guard cells of a leaf swell and the stomata open.
terms.art: Two bean-shaped cells bending apart to open a hole in the middle, and the same two cells pressed together and shut.

terms.meaning: The tubes that carry water and dissolved minerals from the roots up to the leaves.
terms.example: The strings in a celery stalk are bundles of xylem.
terms.art: A cut celery stalk with the strings picked out in blue ink.

terms.meaning: The tubes that carry sweet sap, made in the leaves, to the roots, fruits and growing tips.
terms.example: Sweet neera from a cut coconut flower stalk is phloem sap.
terms.art: A coconut palm with a clay pot tied under a cut flower stalk, dripping with pale sweet sap.

terms.meaning: How salty water or soil is.
terms.example: Sea water has a salinity of about 35 grams of salt in every litre.
terms.art: Three glasses of water labelled fresh, a little salty and sea strength, with piles of salt beside them.

terms.meaning: A tree or shrub that grows in salty water along coasts and river mouths.
terms.example: The Sundarbans in West Bengal is the biggest mangrove forest in the world.
terms.art: Mangrove trees standing on tall arched roots in muddy water at low tide, with a small boat passing.

explanations.concept: Water has a grip: some water is held tightly
explanations.definition: Water is held by the things around it. Some water is held loosely and moves easily. Some is held tightly and is very hard to pull away. In this unit, a pull number says how tightly water is held. A bigger pull number means a tighter hold.
explanations.description: Plain water in a glass is held very loosely. Its pull number is 0. Water in the thin film around a grain of soil is held more tightly, because the grain attracts it. Water with salt or sugar dissolved in it is held more tightly too, because the dissolved bits attract water. Scientists call this idea water potential. They measure it in megapascals, written MPa, and put a minus sign in front. We leave the minus sign out, so a bigger number is a tighter grip. Here are some typical numbers. Wet soil is about 0.1. A leaf cell is about 1 to 1.5. Sea water is about 2.5. Water always moves from the place with the smaller pull number to the place with the bigger one. So 'wet' does not tell you if a root can drink. The grip does.
examples: Plain tap water has a pull number of about 0, so it is easy to take.
A handful of damp soil that you squeeze still holds water you cannot squeeze out. That water is held tightly.
Sea water is about 2.5, which is tighter than the 1 to 1.5 inside most leaf cells.
explanations.art: Three jars: plain water, a soil grain with a thin water film, and salty water. Each has a small hand gripping the water, with the grip drawn tighter from left to right.

explanations.concept: Osmosis: water crosses a thin skin toward the tighter grip
explanations.definition: Osmosis is the movement of water through a thin skin, called a membrane, from the side where water is held more loosely to the side where it is held more tightly. The membrane lets water through but holds back many dissolved things.
explanations.description: Every plant cell has a membrane, and a stiff wall outside it. Inside the cell is a sap with sugars and salts dissolved in it. If the water outside holds water more loosely than the sap does, water flows in. The cell swells and pushes on its wall, like air in a tyre. That firm push is called turgor, and it keeps a leaf standing up. If the outside holds water more tightly, as with salt on a cucumber slice, water flows out. The cell shrinks and goes soft. Many soft cells together make a plant wilt. The wall pushes back as the cell fills. The flow stops when the push-back is as strong as the pull. Then the cell is full and firm.
examples: Salt on cucumber slices pulls water out of the slices, so a puddle forms and the slices go limp.
A wilted coriander sprig stood in water takes water in through its cut end and cells, and goes firm again.
A dry moong seed swells in water because its cells hold water tightly and pull it in.
explanations.art: Two cells in cross-section. In one, blue arrows cross the thin skin into a plump full cell. In the other, arrows leave a shrunken cell that has pulled away from its wall.

explanations.concept: How a root takes water in
explanations.definition: A root takes in water through thousands of thin root hairs. Water flows in when the root's cells hold water more tightly than the soil does.
explanations.description: Behind the tip of each young root, single cells grow out into root hairs. They are so thin that they slip between soil grains, and they make the root's surface huge. One rye plant, grown in a box of soil and carefully measured in 1937, had about 14 billion root hairs. Laid end to end, they would be over 10,000 kilometres long. The root's cells keep their sap thick with sugars and minerals, so they hold water tightly. The plant spends energy to pump minerals into her root cells, and water follows the minerals in. When the soil dries, a plant makes her root sap even thicker, so she can still win water from soil that holds it tightly. The water crosses the root to the xylem. A waxy band around the xylem stops water sneaking past between the cells, so every drop must go through a cell skin. That is how the root decides what gets in.
examples: A moong sprout grown on a wet cloth shows a white fuzz of root hairs under a magnifying glass.
Roots of a potted tulsi that dries out grow thicker sap, which is why a plant that has dried a little can drink from soil that looked too dry.
Pulling a weed leaves the root hairs behind in the soil, which is why a transplanted seedling needs shade and extra water for a few days.
explanations.art: A magnified young root with a fuzz of root hairs reaching between soil grains, and a cut-away showing blue water crossing the root cells into a central tube.

explanations.concept: Fungus helpers: reaching water a root cannot reach
explanations.definition: Mycorrhiza is a partnership between a plant's roots and a fungus. The fungus grows threads, thinner than root hairs, out into the soil and brings back water and minerals. The plant gives the fungus sugar.
explanations.description: About 7 or 8 in every 10 kinds of land plants have fungus partners. The fungal threads reach into tiny gaps that even a root hair cannot enter, and they spread far from the root. In return, the plant sends part of the sugar she makes down to the fungus. Water and minerals travel one way, and sugar travels the other. Scientists are still finding how much water the fungus really brings in different soils.
examples: Most trees in a forest share fungal threads under the soil.
Many crop plants, such as maize and finger millet, grow better with fungus partners in poor soil.
explanations.art: A plant root wrapped in fine white fungal threads that spread out into soil, with blue drops travelling in along the threads and golden dots travelling out.

explanations.concept: The slope from soil to sky
explanations.definition: Water in a plant moves along a slope of pull numbers. It starts in wet soil, where the number is small. It passes through the root, the stem and the leaf, and ends in the air outside, where the number is large.
explanations.description: Here are rounded example numbers. Wet soil is 0.1. A root cell is 0.5. The xylem in the stem is 1. A leaf cell is 1.5. Moist air at 90 percent humidity is about 14. Dry air at 50 percent humidity is about 94. Water flows down this slope because each step has a slightly bigger number. Look at the last step. The drop from the leaf to dry air is about 60 times bigger than all the steps in the plant put together. So the air does nearly all the pulling. Lifting water against gravity costs only about 0.1 for every 10 metres of height. Even for a tree 100 metres tall, that is small next to what dry air offers. In fog, the air is about 99 percent humid and its number is only about 1.4. Then the slope almost vanishes, and a plant loses almost no water. Some tall trees even take in a little water from fog through their leaves.
examples: Washing dries faster on a dry, windy day because dry air pulls water out harder.
A plant loses much less water during a humid monsoon day than on a dry summer afternoon.
A tree 50 metres tall needs only about 0.5 of pull to lift water to the top, which is tiny next to dry air.
explanations.art: A long staircase going down from wet soil through root, stem and leaf, with a tiny step at each stage and a huge cliff at the end where the leaf meets dry air.

explanations.definition: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from a plant, mostly through the stomata, the tiny holes in a leaf. More than 95 of every 100 drops that enter the roots leave this way.
explanations.description: A leaf must open its stomata to let in carbon dioxide, the gas it needs to make food. But when the holes are open, water vapour escapes. Many leaves have 100 to 300 stomata on every square millimetre. Only 1 or 2 drops in every 100 that a plant takes in are used to build her body. The rest passes through the plant and goes into the air. On a hot day, a field of crops sends up about 5 litres of water from each square metre of ground. This is not waste. The water on its way up carries minerals from the soil to the leaves, and its evaporation cools the leaf in the sun, like sweat cools your skin.
examples: A leaf in a closed bag soon has droplets on the inside of the bag.
A grown banyan tree can send hundreds of litres of water into the air on a hot day.
A field of rice needs about 2,500 litres of water for each kilogram of rice, and most of that water passes through the plants.
explanations.art: A magnified leaf section with a stoma open on the underside, blue vapour curling out into the air and tiny dots of carbon dioxide going in.

explanations.concept: Guard cells: a hole that opens by drinking
explanations.definition: Each stoma has two guard cells beside it. When water flows into the guard cells, they swell and bend apart, and the hole opens. When water flows out, they straighten and the hole shuts.
explanations.description: In morning light, the guard cells pump potassium, a mineral, into themselves. Their sap gets thicker, so water flows in by osmosis. They swell, and the thin inner wall of each guard cell is bent open like a bow. When the plant is short of water, her roots and leaves make a signal chemical called abscisic acid. It makes the guard cells let their potassium out. Water follows out, the guard cells go soft, and the hole shuts. At night most stomata shut. A plant must balance two needs: let in carbon dioxide, and not lose too much water. How a leaf weighs that balance, minute by minute, is still being studied.
examples: On a hot afternoon, a bean plant closes many of her stomata to save water.
In bright light and moist soil, the stomata of a leaf are mostly open.
When a cut leaf wilts quickly, its guard cells have lost water and the holes have closed.
explanations.art: Two pictures of a stoma. In the first, two plump bean-shaped guard cells have bent apart to leave a round hole. In the second, two flat guard cells are pressed together with no gap.

explanations.definition: Salty soil water has a big pull number. If it is bigger than the pull number of the root's cells, a root cannot take water in, and water flows out of the root instead.
explanations.description: Sea water has about 35 grams of salt in every litre. Its pull number is about 2.5. A leaf cell of most crop plants is about 1 to 1.5, and a root cell is lower still. So sea water holds its water tighter than the plant does. Water flows out of the roots, and the plant wilts in the middle of a flood. The same thing happens in two other ways. Too much fertiliser is a kind of salt, and it can 'burn' a pot plant. And in dry places, water from canals or wells has a little salt in it. When that water evaporates from a field, the salt stays behind and slowly builds up in the soil. Salt also does a second harm. Some of it gets into the plant and damages her cells over days and weeks. Farmers fix salty soil by washing the salt down with fresh water, by building drains, and by growing crops that tolerate salt.
examples: A pot plant given a spoon of fertiliser, instead of a pinch, droops the next day.
After a cyclone pushes sea water over a field, the paddy droops even when the field is wet.
A white crust on the soil of a dry field is salt left behind after water evaporated.
explanations.art: A flooded paddy field after a storm with seedlings drooping, a white salt crust on the bund, and an arrow showing water leaving a root hair into the salty mud.

explanations.concept: Winning the contest: mangroves and other salt-tolerant plants
explanations.definition: A salt-tolerant plant has a way to hold water tighter than salty water does, and a way to deal with the salt. Mangroves do this in sea water. Each kind has its own method.
explanations.description: Mangroves live where rivers meet the sea, as in the Sundarbans and at Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu. Their leaf and root cells hold water far tighter than 2.5, so they can pull water out of sea water. Most Rhizophora mangroves keep out more than 90 of every 100 grains of salt at the root. The water in their xylem is nearly fresh. Avicennia mangroves let some salt in and push it out through salt glands on their leaves. You can see white crystals on the leaf surface. Some mangroves store salt in old leaves, which then fall off. Their roots stand up out of the mud, because mud has little air. Other salt-tolerant plants include the coconut palm and the Pokkali rice of Kerala, which grows in fields that sea water enters.
examples: Avicennia leaves can have a white dusting of salt that tastes salty.
Pokkali rice in Kerala is grown in salty paddies and fish are farmed in the same fields after harvest.
A coconut palm grows on a beach where most other trees cannot.
explanations.art: A mangrove tree with arched stilt roots standing in sea water, with a drawing of a root tip where only water drops pass through and salt grains are turned away.

explanations.concept: The second river: sugar travels in the phloem
explanations.definition: The xylem carries water up. The phloem is a second set of tubes that carries sugary sap from the leaves to every part of the plant that needs food. Phloem and xylem lie side by side in the stem.
explanations.description: In the 1670s, the Italian scientist Marcello Malpighi cut a ring of bark off a branch. Bark holds the phloem. The leaves above the ring stayed green, because the xylem inside the wood still brought water up. But the bark swelled above the ring, because sugar was stuck there. This shows two pipes. A leaf makes sugar and pumps it into the phloem. Water follows the sugar in by osmosis, so the pressure at the leaf rises and pushes the sap along. The sap flows toward a root, a fruit or a growing tip, where the sugar is taken out and used or stored. The water then goes back into the xylem. The sweet neera that drips from a cut coconut or palmyra flower stalk is phloem sap. An idea of this kind was first written down by Ernst Münch in 1930, and it is still tested today.
examples: Neera from a cut coconut flower stalk is sweet because it is phloem sap.
A tree with a ring of bark cut right round the trunk slowly dies from the roots, because sugar cannot get down to them.
Sugarcane stores its sweet sap in the stem.
explanations.art: A cut-away of a stem showing blue upward tubes in the middle and golden downward tubes in the bark, and a ring cut through the bark with golden sap swelling above the cut.

agreed.text: Water moves through a plant cell's skin toward the side where water is held more tightly. This is called osmosis.
agreed.evidence: Scientists in the 1800s sealed sugar solutions in membrane bags and watched water flow in. Wilhelm Pfeffer measured the pressure in 1877. Plant cells shrink in strong salt and swell in plain water under the microscope.

agreed.text: More than 95 of every 100 drops of water that enter a plant leave through the leaves as vapour.
agreed.evidence: Stephen Hales weighed plants and their water in the 1720s. Modern gas meters on single leaves give the same answer.

agreed.text: Salty soil makes it hard or impossible for most crop plants to take in water.
agreed.evidence: Seeds sprout less and less as salt rises in field and lab trials. Salt-affected farmland has lower yields in India and across the world.

agreed.text: The holes in a leaf open and close because the guard cells around them swell and shrink with water.
agreed.evidence: Under a microscope, guard cells swell and shut in a few minutes when light, dryness or a plant signal chemical changes.

agreed.text: Dry air can pull on a leaf's water far harder than is needed to lift water to the top of the tallest trees.
agreed.evidence: The pull in dry air at 50 percent humidity works out to about 94 on our scale. Lifting water 100 metres needs about 1.

agreed.text: Water goes up in the xylem, and sugar travels in the phloem, which is a different set of tubes.
agreed.evidence: Cutting a ring of bark stops sugar but not water. Aphid feeding and radioactive-labelled sugars show where the sugar flows.

challenging.claim: Water always flows from the wetter place to the drier place.
challenging.for: Water runs downhill and soaks into dry cloth, so it seems to go from wet to dry.
challenging.against: Across a plant cell's skin, water flows toward the side where it is held more tightly, even if that side already has salt. 'Wet' hides the grip.

challenging.claim: Salt kills a plant because salt is a poison.
challenging.for: Some salt does get in and harms cells over time, and a plant with too much salt in her leaves burns at the edges.
challenging.against: Seeds stop sprouting in salty water before much salt enters. A harmless dissolved chemical that is not salt can have the same effect. The first harm is thirst. The poison comes later.

challenging.claim: All mangroves get rid of salt in the same way.
challenging.for: Many mangrove pictures show white salt crystals on leaves.
challenging.against: Rhizophora mangroves keep most salt out at the root. Avicennia mangroves push salt out through their leaves. Others store salt in old leaves. Each kind has its own method.

challenging.claim: The roots are the engine that pushes water up to the leaves.
challenging.who: Many students and some older books.
challenging.for: Roots really can push a little. At night, sap can ooze from a cut stem, which is called root pressure.
challenging.against: A cut stem with no roots still lifts water to its leaves. Root pressure is far too weak to lift water to the top of a tall tree. The pull from the leaves does the lifting.

challenging.claim: A flooded field kills plants only because the roots drown for lack of air.
challenging.for: Water-filled soil has little air, and most roots need oxygen.
challenging.against: Rice survives fresh water floods for days. Sea water floods kill rice much faster, which shows that the salt matters as well as the missing air.

big_questions.q: A plant standing in a flooded, salty field can die of thirst. Is that soil wet or dry?
big_questions.hint: Think about the words 'wet' and 'available to drink'. Are they the same?

big_questions.q: Water moves to where it is held more tightly. Who is doing the pulling, the water or the thing that holds it?
big_questions.hint: Think about a wet sponge and a wet cloth. Which gives up its water more easily?

big_questions.q: Dry air pulls water out of leaves far harder than the tallest tree needs. So is a tree lifting her water, or is the air lifting it?
big_questions.hint: Imagine a tree on a day with no wind and fog. What happens to the water in her tubes?

big_questions.q: A person who drinks sea water gets thirstier, but a mangrove grows in it. Is sea water good or bad for life?
big_questions.hint: Think about who is drinking. Does 'good' belong to the water, or to the one who meets it?

big_questions.q: In dry places, farmers water their fields for years and the soil slowly turns white with salt. Where does the salt come from, and who is to blame?
big_questions.hint: Think about what stays behind when water evaporates.

big_questions.q: Rain that fell on the Western Ghats may pass through many plants before it reaches the sea. Whose water is it?
big_questions.hint: Follow one drop from a cloud, to soil, to a root, to a leaf, and back to the air.

big_questions.q: Nobody can see the pull inside a tree. How could you measure it, and how would you know your measurement was right?
big_questions.hint: Think about how you measure a pull on a spring.

big_questions.q: When soil dries, a plant makes her root sap thicker so she can keep drinking. Is that a decision? How would you find out?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you do when you feel thirsty, and what a root does.

story.title: Water Everywhere, and Not a Drop
story.note: A made-up story. Moushumi, her family and the village are imagined. The science in it is real: sea water floods do leave rice seedlings wilting, fresh rain does wash salt down and out, and Nona is a real traditional salt-tolerant rice of the Bengal coast.
text: On Gosaba island in the Sundarbans, the storm came in the night. Moushumi lay on the floor of the school building with fifty other people and listened to the roof shake. In the morning the wind had gone. But the sea had come over the mud wall that kept the fields dry, and it had left itself behind. Brown water lay across the whole island, up to a grown-up's knees.

It took two days to drain away. On the third day, Moushumi walked to the nursery bed behind her house. This was where her family kept rice seedlings, ready to plant out when the rains came. When she left, they had been bright green. Now every seedling was bent over, with yellow tips, like seedlings in the worst heat of April. The mud around them was wet. She pushed a finger in, and water came up around it.

Her uncle, Bhaskar Kaka, was already there with a bucket. 'They are thirsty,' he said. He dipped the bucket in the pond at the edge of the field and poured it over the bed. The next morning, the seedlings were worse. He poured again.

Moushumi did not understand. The bed was soaked, and her uncle was giving it more water. How could a plant standing in wet mud be thirsty? 'Maybe they drowned,' said her cousin Rupa. But the bed had drained, and drowned plants do not look like plants in a drought.

That evening, her grandmother, Thakuma, sat on the step with a heap of bitter gourd. She cut it into thin rounds, threw handfuls of salt over it and left it in a steel plate. 'Why salt?' Moushumi asked. 'To bring out the bitter water,' said Thakuma. 'My mother did it, and hers.' When Moushumi came back after a while, a green puddle had gathered under the rounds, and the slices had gone soft.

She looked at the puddle for a long time. In class, Ranu Didi had done the same with cucumber. Salt does not make water, Didi had said. Salt holds water, so tightly that the cucumber lets go. Moushumi licked her finger, dipped it in the pond water, and licked it again. Salt. The sea had filled that pond.

She thought of the roots in the bed, sitting in mud soaked with the sea. If salt could pull water out of a gourd, it could pull water out of a root. The mud was wet, and still it held its water too tightly to give any away. The seedlings stood in water and could not drink a drop. And every bucket from the pond made the grip tighter.

She wanted to be sure before she spoke, because who listens to a girl of ten? So she tested it. She dug up six seedlings and washed their roots. She stood three in a cup of pond water and three in a cup of rain water from the drum on the roof. Rupa kept watch. By dusk, the three in the pond water were lying over the rim. The three in the rain water still stood straight.
She carried both cups into the courtyard. Her uncle looked at the cups. He looked at the brown pond. Then he sat down on his heels. 'I have been giving them the sea,' he said quietly.

There was a long argument that night. Where would fresh water come from, when the pond was salty and the tube-well was far away? Thakuma settled it. 'The rain is coming,' she said. 'Rain is the one water with no salt in it. Let it fall on the bed and run off, and it will carry the salt away.' The women of the lane dug a cut in the bank so the water could drain out, and then they waited.

The rain came three days later and fell all night. In the morning, the bed was running with muddy water through the cut, and when Moushumi touched the mud to her tongue, it tasted of nothing. A week later, new leaves pushed up. Many of the old seedlings never recovered. So Thakuma took down a rusty tin from the shelf. Inside were seeds of nona, the old salty-field rice her own mother had grown. 'This kind has met the sea before,' she said. They sowed it in the bed.

On the way to school, Moushumi crossed the creek. The mangroves along its bank stood in the dark water, as green as ever. The storm had passed right over them. The sea had stood around their roots for two days, and not one leaf drooped. She stopped on the bridge. Whatever those trees knew, they were drinking from the very water that had hurt her seedlings.
'How?' she said aloud. A fish jumped, and the ripples spread out, and the tide began to turn.
story.epiphany: A root drinks only when her cells hold water more tightly than the soil does. Salty mud holds water so tightly that seedlings in a wet bed were still thirsty, and pouring on salty pond water made the grip even tighter. Fresh rain washed the salt away and loosened the grip.
ask: Why did the seedlings droop even though the mud was wet?
Why did pouring on more pond water make them worse?
How could Moushumi's test with the two cups be made fairer, so that nobody could argue with it?
art: Gosaba island after a storm: brown water across the fields, a school building on higher ground, and women wading with pots on their heads.
A nursery bed of rice seedlings bent over in wet mud, with Moushumi pressing one finger into the mud.
A grandmother on a doorstep tossing salt over thin rounds of bitter gourd on a steel plate, with a green puddle forming, and a girl watching closely.
Two clay cups in a courtyard at dusk: three seedlings flopped over the rim of one, three standing straight in the other, and a man crouching to look.

games.title: Which Way Does the Water Go?
games.context: This is a guessing game about the pull numbers from this unit. Each card shows two places and their pull numbers. You guess which way the water moves, and say why.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a pile in the middle of a table, and four players each holding two tokens marked Toward A and Toward B.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One card held up by the reader, with two places A and B and a pull number for each, and the back hidden against the reader's chest.
