roots.context: We have tested salt, seeds and leaves, and followed water from the soil to the sky. Now we ask what this tells us about thirst, about wet and dry, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Water does not go where there is the most water, but where it is held most tightly. A root can drink only if her cells hold water tighter than the soil does. Salty soil holds water very tightly, so a plant can stand in a flooded field and still die of thirst.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'wet' and 'dry' as if they only measured how much water there is, and as if more water always means more to drink. But water has a grip. Water in salty mud, or in a thin film on soil grains, is held so tightly that a root cannot pull it free.
deep_truth.evidence: In the sprout test, every cup got the same damp towel and the same amount of water. The seeds sprouted in plain water, sprouted fewer and slower with a little salt, and not at all in strong salt water. Salt on cucumber slices pulled water out of them in the same way.

three.who_am_i: Your own cells are salty inside, and that is how they keep their water. If you drink sea water, you lose water and get thirstier. The same rule that dries a seedling in the sea is working in you.
three.what_is_life: A mangrove keeps salt out at her roots. A sea fish drinks sea water and pushes the salt out through her gills. Different living things found different ways to win the same contest over water.
three.what_is_this_world: Rain, soil, a root, a leaf and dry air are not five kinds of water. It is one water, moving down one long slope from the ground to the sky.

roots.thread: A drop of water in wet soil, in a root, in a leaf and in the air is the same drop on a long journey. The drop goes toward wherever it is held more tightly, step by step, and the biggest step of all is the last one, from the leaf into dry air. A plant cannot stop this slope. She can only change the grip, by thickening her sap, shutting a leaf hole or keeping salt out at the root. So each plant is a place where the water's long slope from the sea, to the cloud, to the soil, to the sky passes through a living body.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to put a lump of salt in water at night, and to bring it back in the morning. Shvetaketu cannot find it. Uddalaka tells him to sip from the top, the middle and the bottom. It is salty everywhere. The salt is there even though no one can see it.
teachings.link: Dissolved salt cannot be seen, yet it decides where the water goes. In a cucumber, a seed or a root, what you cannot see still controls what you can.

teachings.source: Rig Veda 10.9.1 to 10.9.3 (the hymn to the Waters)
teachings.teaching: The Waters are asked to share their kindest sap, as loving mothers share with their children, and are praised as givers of strength and healing.
teachings.link: Water brings its sap, the minerals and sugars, to every part of a plant. The hymn saw water as the thing that carries life from one being to another.

science.text: Water moves from higher to lower water potential in every living thing, in plants, fungi, bacteria and animals. The same rule governs a root, a mushroom and a kidney.
Whether a plant thickening her root sap in dry soil is making a decision is a question scientists describe in different words, and it is still being asked.

other_view.view: When the soil dries, a root's cells fill with more sugars and salts because chemical signals switch genes on. That is chemistry running by itself. Saying the plant 'decides' is only a way of talking.

practice.title: The water you cannot squeeze out
practice.say: Wet a clean cloth and hold it in both hands. Squeeze it gently and let the water drip into a bowl. Then squeeze as hard as you can. Notice that the cloth is still damp. Breathe in slowly, and breathe out slowly, three times. Think of the damp that stays in the cloth. Some water stays held, however hard you squeeze.
practice.kid: Wet a cloth. Squeeze it hard over a bowl. Feel that it is still damp. Breathe slowly three times. Some water stays held.

ask: If a root cannot drink from wet soil because the soil holds on too tightly, was there water there or not?
A mangrove and the sea both hold on to water. Is the contest fair? Who is winning, and does anyone lose?
A plant thickens her sap when the soil dries. Is she deciding, or is it just happening? How could you ever tell the difference?

how_we_found_out.story: In 1894, Henry Dixon and John Joly, two scientists in Dublin, said that a tree pulls her water up from the top, and that the water holds together in an unbroken thread under strain. Many scientists did not believe it. A pulled thread of water, they said, should snap. And nobody could measure the pull inside a living tree. In the early 1960s, Per Scholander, a Norwegian-born scientist working in the United States, found a way. He cut a leafy twig and sealed it in a metal chamber, with the cut end poking out. Then he slowly raised the gas pressure around the leaves. When a drop of sap just showed at the cut end, the gas pressure matched how hard the twig had been pulling its water. He measured pulls many times stronger than the pressure of the air around us. The thread of water had not snapped. Scientists still argue about some details.
how_we_found_out.who: Per Scholander (1905 to 1980), a Norwegian-born scientist working in the United States, building on Henry Dixon and John Joly of Dublin
how_we_found_out.when: 1894 (the idea), and the early 1960s, with results published in 1965 (the measurement)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists thought a thread of water pulled so hard must snap, so the pull idea could not be right. Scholander measured the pull and found that plants hold water under strong pull without it breaking.

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home, so the amounts below are estimates to check. Salt and the Sprouts: salt strengths of about 0.75, 1.5 and 3 percent were chosen so moong germination falls in steps. Expect something like 9 or 10, 6 to 9, 1 to 6 and 0 or 1 sprouts, but results vary by seed batch. If cup A also fails, the seeds are old, so try a fresh packet. Fan, Still Air or Bag: the oil layer and the narrow bottle neck make small losses visible, and the drop may be only 1 to 5 millimetres. Leave it overnight if it is small. A kitchen scale gives a second reading. The bag usually shows droplets within 2 hours. Salted Slices: expect about 1 to 3 teaspoons of liquid on the salt plate after 20 minutes, and less on the sugar plate. Leave the Salt Behind: a white crust forms along the upper edge of the wet part of the salty strip in about a day, and may take longer in humid weather. String Staircase: the 94 centimetre strip needs a table or floor space. The pull numbers are rounded examples. Rescue the Salty Pot: soil with salt flushed by 600 millilitres usually sprouts methi and the unflushed cup usually does not, but a very salty or very clay soil may need more water. Which Way Does the Water Go: all 24 cards and 8 tokens are written out, and the solo version scores out of 48.
